subject: World Literature & Translated Short Stories
notes: Anthology of masterpiece world short stories translated into Tangkhul by TLS scholars. Includes Tolstoy's 'Where Love Is, God Is', Maupassant's 'The Necklace', and O. Henry's 'Gift of the Magi'.

front_matter.title_page: Duniyawui Khararchan Kathara: World Classic Stories Translated into Tangkhul (1991)
front_matter.preface: This anthology introduced Tangkhul secondary students to three monumental gems of world narrative prose. The translations demonstrate the narrative flexibility of modern standard Tangkhul, handling 19th-century Russian spiritual realism, French bourgeois tragedy, and American ironic compassion with equal brilliance.

chapters.title: Where Love Is, God Is (Khanganing kala Varivara) -- Leo Tolstoy
chapters.summary: Martin Avdeitch the cobbler looking for Christ and finding Him in the freezing stranger, hungry mother, and apple boy.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 1: Martin Avdeitch kaho shoemaker akhana khong-ngaching shimli pamsai. Ana zingsho pupup Lairik Kathara hanglaga ningkazang kazip-kasaye. Ngazing akha ana khongyui akhata kapeiye: 'Martin! Martin! Yanglu zingsho kashokli I nawui ngalemli rara!' Zingkhamathān shoklakha, Martinna window eina kashikathali yanglakha, Stepan kaho mayarnao kacham kashikaza akha snow ngalungli ngachek-kashung pamsai theitserie. Martinna ali shimsanglaga meikhangahui tharili tea kashak milaga chotkhangashit tui hangmi. Chitharan shanaowon akha awui naonli kachon maleilakha chirzat-lakha theilaga ali kachon kala paisa miye. Ngazing-tharan Martinna theitserie: 'Awui mai eina Christana hung-kachitheisaye: kasakei kachamnaobingli sakasashikahai ot pupup chi ili sakasashisaye!'
chapters.english_translation: In a little basement room in a certain city lived Martin Avdeitch, a cobbler. Every evening he read the Gospels until his heart burned within him. One night he heard a voice calling him: 'Martin, look out into the street tomorrow, for I will come.' Next day, while watching out the window, he saw Stepanitch clearing snow, shivering in rags; he called him in and gave him warm tea. Later he sheltered a poor mother with a child wrapped in thin garments and gave her his cloak and money. At dusk he realized: Christ had indeed visited him that day, for 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.'
grammar_notes: Direct quote attribution in Tangkhul narrative: 'hoda leisai' / 'hoda hang'.
Spiritual realization clause: 'Awui mai eina Christana hung-kachitheisaye'.
exercises: What three people did Martin encounter during the snowy day?
Explain the ethical message of Tolstoy's story.

chapters.title: The Necklace (Khangaphei wui Phasang) -- Guy de Maupassant
chapters.summary: Mathilde Loisel borrowing the diamond necklace, losing it at the ball, and toiling ten years for a tragic revelation.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 2: Mathilde Loisel kaho ngalashana kaphā akha pamsai; kha ana kashang-phā saphā-kashangli pamei lungkakhui leisai. Ministry-wui grand ball phanitli valakhavai ana awui ngalemwui Madame Forestier eina diamond necklace (phasang) khuiye. Ball phanitli mathat-eina pheichak salaga, shimli hung-kaphung tharan, theilu! Awui phasang chi ngashiman-serie! Mathilde kala awui va-na ten years kuppup kashakashi ot salaga 36,000 francs kashunsangserie phasang kathara khuisangkhavai. Kum thakharā ngaphalaga ana Madame Forestierli champsangie; chitharan Forestierna hang: 'Oh, Mathilde! Iwui phasang chi paste (artificial) sai! Awui value 500 francs kacham-sai!'
chapters.english_translation: Mathilde Loisel was a charming woman born into a family of clerks who dreamed of wealth and luxury. Invited to a grand ball at the Ministry, she borrowed a magnificent diamond necklace from her wealthy friend Madame Forestier. She was the belle of the ball, but arriving home, discovered to her horror that the necklace was lost. Rather than admit the loss, she and her husband worked ten grueling years in squalor and debt to purchase a replacement necklace for thirty-six thousand francs. Ten years later, meeting Madame Forestier in the park, aged and haggard, she learned the devastating truth: 'Oh my poor Mathilde! Mine was false! It was worth at most five hundred francs!'
grammar_notes: French loanword handling: francs and ball phonetically adapted in Tangkhul narrative prose.
exercises: Describe Mathilde's character flaws and their consequences.
How does the story highlight the folly of excessive pride?

chapters.title: The Gift of the Magi (Magibingwui Khangashe) -- O. Henry
chapters.summary: Della selling her hair for a watch chain and Jim selling his watch for her hair combs in unconditional sacrificial love.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 3: Della eina Jimna kacham shimli pamsai; Christmas tharili Della-li dollar 1.87 kacham leisai. Awui va Jimli Christmas gift mikhavai, ana awui kaphāmei sam (hair) pashitsanglaga Jimwui gold watch wui platinum chain khuiye. Ngazing-tharan Jimna shimli zanglaga Della-wui sam katat theilaga ngachekserie: kasakei Jimna awui gold watch pashitsanglaga Della-wui sam kaphā kachikhavai tortoise-shell combs khuisang-kahaisai! Athum khaniwui gift ngashiman thada theilashu, athumna magibing thada kaphāmei khangayei eina kashang thotna.
chapters.english_translation: One dollar and eighty-seven cents was all Della had on Christmas Eve to buy a present for her husband Jim. In sacrificial devotion, she sold her glorious cascading brown hair for twenty dollars to purchase a platinum fob chain for Jim's prized gold watch. When Jim returned home, he stared at her shorn hair in stunned amazement: for he had sold his gold watch to purchase the expensive set of tortoiseshell combs Della had long coveted! Though their material treasures were made temporarily useless, they were the wisest of all who give gifts--they were the Magi.

pages.title: The Gift of the Magi (Magibingwui Khangashe) -- O. Henry
lines: CHAPTER 3: THE GIFT OF THE MAGI (MAGIBINGWUI KHANGASHE) -- O. HENRY
Summary: Della selling her hair for a watch chain and Jim selling his watch for her hair ...
Khararchan 3: Della eina Jimna kacham shimli pamsai; Christmas tharili
Della-li dollar 1.87 kacham leisai. Awui va Jimli Christmas gift
mikhavai, ana awui kaphāmei sam (hair) pashitsanglaga Jimwui gold watch
wui platinum chain khuiye. Ngazing-tharan Jimna shimli zanglaga Della-
wui sam katat theilaga ngachekserie: kasakei Jimna awui gold watch
pashitsanglaga Della-wui sam kaphā kachikhavai tortoise-shell combs
khuisang-kahaisai! Athum khaniwui gift ngashiman thada theilashu,
athumna magibing thada kaphāmei khangayei eina kashang thotna.
One dollar and eighty-seven cents was all Della had on Christmas Eve to
buy a present for her husband Jim. In sacrificial devotion, she sold her
glorious cascading brown hair for twenty dollars to purchase a platinum
fob chain for Jim's prized gold watch. When Jim returned home, he stared
at her shorn hair in stunned amazement: for he had sold his gold watch
to purchase the expensive set of tortoiseshell combs Della had long
coveted! Though their material treasures were made temporarily useless,
they were the wisest of all who give gifts--they were the Magi.
